title: Normal Modes in Polyatomic Molecules
lead: A molecule of N atoms has 3N degrees of freedom, and the ones left after translation and rotation are its vibrations. The motions of a group of atoms have names of their own, and normal coordinates rewrite the vibrational energy one mode at a time, with CO as the simplest case.
notes: Shared under the book's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; the six Wikipedia animations of Figure 13.9.1, used by the book with permission, are not shown.

exercises.source_id: 3N – 6 degrees of vibrational freedom for a nonlinear molecule
exercises.prompt: Acetylene, HC≡CH, is linear and formaldehyde, H₂CO, is planar but not linear. For each molecule, how many of its degrees of freedom are rotational and how many are vibrational?

parts.hint: Count the atoms first, then use Table 13.9.1.

answer.solution: Each molecule has four atoms, so $3N = 12$ degrees of freedom, three of them translational. Acetylene is linear, so it has only two rotational degrees of freedom and $3N - 5 = 3(4) - 5 = 7$ vibrational ones. Formaldehyde is nonlinear, so it has three rotational degrees of freedom and $3N - 6 = 3(4) - 6 = 6$ vibrational ones. The extra vibration of acetylene is the price of losing a rotation about its axis: its two bends come in perpendicular pairs.

footnotes.html: The book swaps the two labels: the orientation in space is set by the rotational degrees of freedom, and the position of the center of mass by the translational ones.
“Is equation to” means “is equal to”: $q = \Delta r(\mathrm{C}) + \Delta r(\mathrm{O})$.

derivations.what: the vibrational energy of a polyatomic molecule
derivations.source: Physical Chemistry (LibreTexts), 13.9 Normal Modes in Polyatomic Molecules

then.why: The kinetic energy of each normal coordinate is that of a single particle of reduced mass $\kmu_j$ moving along $\kQj$.

nodes.note: The book writes the reduced mass of the kinetic term as $\mu_i$; it belongs to mode $j$, $\mu_j$.
The book prints the potential's sum over $j$ inside the sum over $j$, and mixes $\mu_j$ with $Q_i$. Each mode's operator holds only its own kinetic and potential terms, as written here.

assumes.text: The total wavefunction is a product of the individual wavefunctions and the energy is the sum of independent energies.

steps.cap: Each $\hat{H}_{vib,j}$ acts on $Q_j$ alone, so a product of one-mode wavefunctions splits the equation into one equation for each mode.

nodes.note: The book prints the first line as $\psi_{vib} = Q_1, Q_2, Q_3 ..., Q_{vib}$; it means the wavefunction of all the normal coordinates, $\psi_{vib}(Q_1, Q_2, \ldots, Q_{N_{vib}})$.

then.why: With the product wavefunction each mode contributes its own energy $E_j$.

steps.cap: Each $\hat{H}_{vib,j}$ is a harmonic oscillator in $Q_j$, with the levels of the harmonic oscillator.

nodes.note: The book's upper limit reads $N_{vin}$; it is $N_{vib}$.
